title: Warm Up Routines
description: The four key components of a warm up and the physiological and psychological benefits of warming up before sport.
content_html:
Why Warm Up?

A warm up is one of the most effective single actions an athlete can take to reduce their injury risk. The R180 specification covers both the key components (2.1) and the physiological and psychological benefits (2.2) — and you are expected to apply both to specific sporting scenarios. Failing to warm up is not a neutral act: it measurably increases injury risk by leaving muscles cold, joints stiff and the mind unprepared for the demands of competition.

Phase 1: Pulse Raising (2.1.1)

The first component is pulse raising — low-to-moderate intensity continuous activity that gradually elevates heart rate, breathing rate and core body temperature. Examples include jogging around the pitch, light cycling or steady swimming. The purpose is to increase blood flow and oxygen delivery to the working muscles before the intensity of the session increases. Starting sport at a resting heart rate without a pulse raiser leaves muscles starved of the oxygen and blood flow needed for efficient contraction, dramatically increasing the risk of muscle strains. Duration is typically 5 to 10 minutes.

Phase 2: Mobility (2.1.1)

Mobility exercises are controlled, rhythmic movements that take joints through their full range of motion — for example, arm circles, hip rotations and ankle rolls. They differ from stretching in that mobility work focuses on joint movement rather than muscle lengthening. Following the pulse raiser, mobility work reduces joint stiffness and increases the production of synovial fluid, which lubricates the joint surfaces and reduces the friction that could otherwise contribute to cartilage wear. For a basketball player, mobility work targeting the shoulder, hip and ankle joints is particularly important before the explosive jumping, pivoting and shooting demands of the game.

Key Fact

The four key components of a warm up in the R180 specification are: (1) pulse raising, (2) mobility, (3) dynamic stretching, and (4) skill rehearsal phase. They are performed in this order — from low intensity to sport-specific activity.

Phase 3: Dynamic Stretching (2.1.1)

Dynamic stretching involves moving through a full range of motion in a controlled way — leg swings, walking lunges, arm swings and high knees are all examples. Unlike static stretching (which is held in a fixed position and is reserved for the cool down), dynamic stretching during the warm up maintains the elevated muscle temperature achieved during pulse raising while progressively lengthening the muscles. Research shows that static stretching before sport can temporarily reduce muscle power output — this is why dynamic stretching has replaced it as the warm-up standard. Dynamic stretching directly increases muscle flexibility and pliability of ligaments and tendons, reducing the chance of strains and sprains during the main activity.

Phase 4: Skill Rehearsal Phase (2.1.1)

The final component is the skill rehearsal phase, which bridges the general preparation of the earlier components with the specific demands of the sport. A netball player might practise passing drills, receiving and shooting; a sprinter might perform acceleration runs at 70%, 80% and then 95% of maximum effort. The skill rehearsal phase also activates the neuromuscular pathways — the communication between the brain and the muscles — so that movement patterns are crisp and reactive when the game begins. Crucially, it links directly to the psychological benefits of a warm up: practising skills in a controlled environment before competition increases confidence and concentration.

Key Fact

The six physiological benefits of a warm up are: increase in muscle temperature, increase in heart rate, increase in flexibility of muscles and joints, increase in pliability of ligaments and tendons, increase in blood flow and oxygen to muscles, and increase in the speed of muscle contraction.

The specification (2.2.2) lists five psychological benefits: the ability to heighten or control arousal levels; improved concentration and focus; increased motivation; increased confidence; and mental rehearsal. The skill rehearsal phase is the component most directly responsible for these psychological gains — practising skills successfully at the end of a warm up builds confidence and sharpens focus. Controlling arousal is particularly important: a nervous performer can use the warm up to regulate their activation level, using techniques such as controlled breathing or imagery to arrive at the optimum psychological state for performance. These benefits directly reduce injury risk by ensuring the athlete is mentally focused rather than anxious or distracted when the main activity begins.

The specification explicitly asks you to be aware of the negative effects of not warming up. Physiologically: muscles remain cold and less elastic, dramatically increasing the risk of strains; ligaments and tendons are less pliable, raising sprain risk; heart rate and blood pressure rise too rapidly at the start of strenuous exercise, placing cardiovascular stress on the body; and the speed of muscle contraction remains low, reducing reaction time and power. Psychologically: without the skill rehearsal phase, confidence and concentration are lower; arousal may be poorly calibrated — too high (anxiety) or too low (under-arousal) — leading to reckless or sluggish movement. In exam scenarios, describing these "negative effects" is the exact mirror image of the benefits — so learning both together is highly efficient revision.
exam_tip_html: When listing physiological benefits, always begin with the phrase "increase in" — for example, "increase in muscle temperature" — because OCR mark schemes credit the exact specification wording. For a 6-mark question on warm up benefits, cover both physiological and psychological dimensions and link each benefit to a consequence: "an increase in muscle temperature leads to greater elasticity, which reduces the risk of a muscle strain." Simply listing benefits without explaining the mechanism typically scores in the Developing band only.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A complete warm up has four components performed in order: pulse raising, mobility, dynamic stretching, and skill rehearsal — each preparing the body for increasingly sport-specific demands.
  • The six physiological benefits all begin with "increase in" — muscle temperature, heart rate, flexibility, pliability of ligaments and tendons, blood flow and oxygen, and speed of muscle contraction.
  • The five psychological benefits — heightened or controlled arousal, improved concentration, increased motivation, increased confidence and mental rehearsal — reduce the risk of injury by ensuring the athlete is mentally prepared and focused before competition.

glossary_terms.definition: A structured sequence of activities performed before sport or exercise that prepares the body and mind for the demands of performance and reduces injury risk.
Controlled movement exercises that take joints through their full range of motion, used during a warm up to reduce stiffness and prepare joints for the demands of sport.
Stretching performed through controlled movement that mimics the actions of the sport, such as leg swings or walking lunges, rather than holding a fixed position.
The sport-specific part of a warm up in which athletes practise the actual technical skills and movements they will perform during the main activity at progressively increasing intensity.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct order for the key components of a warm up?
A) Mobility, pulse raising, skill rehearsal, dynamic stretching
B) Pulse raising, mobility, dynamic stretching, skill rehearsal
C) Dynamic stretching, pulse raising, mobility, skill rehearsal
D) Skill rehearsal, mobility, dynamic stretching, pulse raising
practice_questions.marks: B) Pulse raising, mobility, dynamic stretching, skill rehearsal [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two physiological benefits of completing a warm up before sport.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct physiological benefits from the specification: increase in muscle temperature / increase in heart rate / increase in flexibility of muscles and joints / increase in pliability of ligaments and tendons / increase in blood flow and oxygen to muscles / increase in the speed of muscle contraction. Answers must identify a specific benefit — "it prepares the body" alone does not score. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why dynamic stretching is preferred over static stretching during a warm up.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. "dynamic stretching is more active"). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. "dynamic stretching maintains the elevated muscle temperature achieved during pulse raising, whereas static stretching held in a fixed position can temporarily reduce muscle power output"). A further developed explanation scores 3 marks (e.g. add "by moving through a full range of motion in a controlled way, dynamic stretching simultaneously improves flexibility and pliability of ligaments and tendons without the power-reducing effect of prolonged static holds"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the purpose of the skill rehearsal phase of a warm up and give one sport-specific example of an activity used in this phase.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): the skill rehearsal phase involves practising the specific technical skills and movements of the sport at progressively increasing intensity, bridging general preparation and the demands of the main activity; it also activates neuromuscular pathways and provides psychological benefits such as increased confidence and focus (2 marks for a clear developed description with the neuromuscular or psychological element included; 1 mark for a basic statement about practising sport skills).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a sprinter performing acceleration runs at 70%, then 80%, then 95% of maximum effort, progressively loading the neuromuscular system and building confidence in their starting technique before the race (2 marks for a sport-specific, progressive example; 1 mark for a vague reference to "practising" without detail). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A school cricket team arrives at the ground 10 minutes before a match. Their coach insists they start play without a warm up.

Discuss the potential negative effects of not warming up on the physiological and psychological readiness of the players.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering physiological negatives (muscles remain cold and less elastic — increased muscle strain risk; ligaments and tendons are less pliable — increased sprain risk; blood flow and oxygen delivery to muscles is low — reduced contraction speed and power; rapid rise in heart rate places cardiovascular stress on the body) alongside psychological negatives (no skill rehearsal — reduced confidence and concentration; poorly calibrated arousal — anxiety or under-arousal likely; no opportunity for mental rehearsal of batting or bowling technique). Both dimensions covered with developed explanation and scenario application.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least one physiological and one psychological negative identified and briefly explained with some reference to cricket.
Developing (2 marks): One or two negatives identified but not developed or applied.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
An athletics coach is designing a warm up routine for a group of 400m runners. She must choose between a full four-component warm up and a shorter version that skips the skill rehearsal phase to save time.

Evaluate the extent to which completing all four components of a warm up is necessary for injury prevention and performance in 400m running.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing that all four components serve distinct purposes — pulse raising increases blood flow and muscle temperature; mobility reduces joint stiffness; dynamic stretching increases pliability and flexibility; skill rehearsal prepares neuromuscular pathways and provides psychological benefits. The counter-argument considers whether 400m running is technically complex enough to require a full skill rehearsal phase (compared to, say, gymnastics), and whether time constraints in a competitive environment justify abbreviating. A clear substantiated judgement is reached — e.g. that the first three components are non-negotiable for injury prevention but the skill rehearsal phase has relatively more value for complex-technique sports.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two components discussed with benefits applied to 400m running, and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points about warm up components largely descriptive rather than evaluative.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about warming up with little development and no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which component of a warm up involves gradually elevating heart rate and breathing rate through low-to-moderate intensity continuous activity?
Which of the following is a psychological benefit of a warm up listed in the R180 specification (2.2.2)?
options: Increase in speed of muscle contraction
Increase in blood flow and oxygen to muscles
Increase in pliability of ligaments and tendons

knowledge_checks.q: Dynamic stretching is performed through _____ movement, rather than holding a fixed position, so that elevated muscle temperature is maintained from the pulse-raising phase.
The skill rehearsal phase of a warm up directly activates _____ pathways, ensuring that communication between the brain and muscles is responsive when the main activity begins.
Match each warm up component to its primary purpose.
right: Increases flexibility and pliability through controlled sport-mimicking movements
Gradually increases heart rate, breathing rate and muscle temperature
Reduces joint stiffness by taking joints through their full range of motion

flashcard_questions.q: What are the four key components of a warm up in the correct order?
flashcard_questions.a: The four components are pulse raising, mobility, dynamic stretching, and skill rehearsal phase, performed in that order from general to sport-specific.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of the pulse-raising component of a warm up?
flashcard_questions.a: Pulse raising gradually increases heart rate, breathing rate and muscle temperature through low-intensity activity, improving blood flow and oxygen delivery to working muscles.

flashcard_questions.q: How do mobility exercises differ from dynamic stretching in a warm up?
flashcard_questions.a: Mobility exercises move joints through their full range to reduce stiffness and increase synovial fluid, while dynamic stretching focuses on lengthening muscles through sport-mimicking movement.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is static stretching not recommended during the warm up phase?
flashcard_questions.a: Static stretching temporarily reduces muscle power output and does not maintain the elevated muscle temperature achieved during pulse raising, so dynamic stretching is preferred.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the six physiological benefits of a warm up listed in the specification.
flashcard_questions.a: Increase in muscle temperature, heart rate, flexibility of muscles and joints, pliability of ligaments and tendons, blood flow and oxygen to muscles, and speed of muscle contraction.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the five psychological benefits of a warm up listed in the specification.
flashcard_questions.a: The five psychological benefits are: heighten or control arousal levels, improve concentration and focus, increase motivation, increase confidence, and mental rehearsal.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the skill rehearsal phase contribute to psychological readiness before competition?
flashcard_questions.a: Practising sport-specific skills successfully at the end of a warm up builds confidence, sharpens concentration and allows athletes to calibrate their arousal to an optimal level.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the risk if an athlete begins strenuous sport without first completing a pulse-raising phase?
flashcard_questions.a: Muscles remain cold and less elastic, dramatically increasing the risk of muscle strains, while heart rate and blood pressure rise too rapidly, placing cardiovascular stress on the body.

flashcard_questions.q: How does an increase in muscle temperature reduce injury risk during sport?
flashcard_questions.a: Warmer muscles are more elastic and contract faster, meaning they can absorb force and respond to sudden demands without tearing, significantly reducing the risk of strains.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the benefit of an increase in pliability of ligaments and tendons as a result of warming up?
flashcard_questions.a: More pliable ligaments and tendons can stretch further without tearing when joints are taken to their limits, directly reducing the risk of sprains during sport.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of a dynamic stretch suitable for a footballer before a match.
flashcard_questions.a: Leg swings — the player stands on one leg and swings the other leg forward and back through a full range of motion, mimicking the kicking action used during play.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the specification say about the possible negative effects of not warming up?
flashcard_questions.a: Without a warm up, muscles are cold and less elastic (raising strain risk), joints are stiff, arousal is poorly calibrated, and confidence and concentration are lower before competition.
